A7R5 Co-IP Help
Hi everyone,
I’m wondering if anyone has done a successful Co-IP in transiently transfected A7R5 cells?
My biggest issues are that even with 2 x 100mm dishes I don’t get a full 1mg of protein in the Lysate, plus getting really low transfection efficiency.
I use a DNA to JetPrime ratio of (1:3), transfecting 10μg per 100mm dish, let the cells transfect for 24 hours then refresh media and let the cells recover for an additional 24 hours, treating them with inhibitor 1 at 16 hours prior to lysis and inhibitor 2 at 4hrs prior to lysis.
Wash cells with cold DPBS
Use ~300-400ul CST 1x lysis buffer (+ 1x PI cocktail) on each dish for 15 min in 4C, Sonicate, and spin down at 4C. Quantify using Pierce BCA assay.
Preclear 500ug of lysate using blank A/G magnetic beads, then transfer Lysate to A/G magnetic beads plus the mouse Myc-tagged Ab (calculated based off the manufacturer 1:250 recommendation for IP). I then let the Lysate rotate overnight at 4C slowly.
Wash beads the next day with the same lysis buffer twice. Add 20ul of 4x Lammeli buffer and boil for 5 min. Run it through 8% SDS Page gel, transfer, block in 5% BSA, and probe overnight with rabbit Ab at 1:4000 (according to trial and error on normal WB and not IP). Then secondary ab 1:5000. When I image I get bands even in the non transfected lanes.
I’ve been struggling with this for a year and desperately need help.
Please any and all help is welcome!

text:
How do you reach US students for a European PhD program? Hoping for some advice
Hi r/labrats,
I hope posts like this are allowed here. If not, mods, feel free to remove it.
I coordinate ORFeus, an EU-funded PhD network (MSCA Doctoral Network) with 15 fully funded PhD positions across Europe. The research is on microproteins and the dark proteome: Ribo-seq, proteomics, immunopeptidomics, AI, etc.
Our problem is that almost no US students apply. Over 10 US professors in the field are helping us: posters on their campuses, emails to their departments, forwarding the call to colleagues and students. We’ve also posted on JobRxiv, the Genetics Society of America, LinkedIn, Indeed, PhDScanner and FindAPhD (and more). Applications are coming in from Europe, Asia and elsewhere, but from the US we get close to nothing. Any nationality can apply, and these are salaried positions with benefits, not stipends.
One thing that did not help at the start is that we mentioned that positions require an MSc or 'equivalent', which is the formal language the EU recommends, but as I have now learned rarely applies to US students. They do a BSc, do some years in lab rotations, etc., and in the end EU institutes can make exceptions for these candidates, as they clearly have that 'equivalent' experience. We changed this in follow-up advertisements, but to no avail.
So I would love to hear from anyone who’s been through this. Students, PhDs, postdocs, PIs: how would you get a call like this in front of US students? And if you’re a student, what would make you skip it?
Thanks a lot, any advice is welcome.
Edit: To clarify, since a few people asked: we are not looking for US students in particular, and nationality plays no role in selection. We simply want to reach as many potentially excellent candidates as possible, wherever they are from, and we get good applicants from many countries worldwide so we are happy to see that there seems to be a global reach. The US is the one place where almost nothing comes in, despite a lot of effort through US colleagues. I am trying to understand whether that is down to our approach, whether it is just to be expected for European PhDs, or whether there is something we could do differently.

H₂O₂ treatment conditions in cell culture
Hi everyone! I have a question about the choice of culture medium for in vitro H₂O₂ treatment experiments.
I’m trying to understand how researchers account for the effects of culture medium composition on the effective H₂O₂ exposure. I’ve read that sodium pyruvate can react with and scavenge H₂O₂, potentially reducing the amount available to the cells. Serum may also affect H₂O₂ stability and reactivity through interactions with proteins and other components.
I’m wondering what conditions researchers typically use during H₂O₂ treatments, particularly when working with relatively low concentrations and longer exposure times.
I’m also unsure whether switching to serum-free, pyruvate-free medium is preferable for controlling H₂O₂ exposure, since serum deprivation itself may introduce stress and confound the results.
For those who have worked with H₂O₂ treatment in cell culture:
- Do you typically use serum-free or serum-containing medium during treatment?
- Do you specifically avoid sodium pyruvate, or do you use standard culture medium containing pyruvate?
-Have you found that serum or other medium components substantially affect your results?
- How do you account for H₂O₂ degradation during longer treatments?
- Are there published protocols that clearly describe the medium composition during H₂O₂ exposure?
I’d especially appreciate references or insights into how researchers choose their treatment conditions and interpret results when the medium itself may affect H₂O₂ exposure, particularly in low-dose, prolonged treatments.
Thanks!

What actually makes a systematic review worth publishing?
Systematic reviews are long-term relationships. They need a lot of commitment, so to make sure it's worth it, you need to filter out the ones not worth pursuing. And it's about two things the question and the data.
It all lies in the gap analysis. The question needs to actually contribute to the corpus of literature out there, something that a guideline can refer to would be ideal. Once you've got your target set, the next best step is to see if there's feasible literature out there.
The best way I found of using AI here is to draft a first-pass evidence spreadsheet with columns in PICO format, with the DOI in a separate column for me to independently verify. If you're gonna use AI in your research, you need to be able to audit every decision it makes with a fine-tooth comb.
There are a few tools I've found that are pretty useful for gap analysis and actually conducting a systematic review (plus meta-analysis when actually feasible), and I'm happy to share what I've learnt just drop me a DM!!! Anyways, I'd love to hear from y'all, what makes a review worth pursuing???

Improving the weight measurement of an object without changing the scale
Suppose you're stuck in a lab with a digital scale and many objects (A, B, C, ...) and your task is to measure the weight of object A as precisely as possible. You can actually improve your estimate by measuring different combinations (A alone, A+B, A+C, B+C, etc.). Because these measurements are all correlated, if you combine them you can improve your uncertainty in A. With just 2 objects and 3 measurements you can reduce the uncertainty by 18%, for example.
I created a repository describing this process in detail. You can use an interactive python program with your own scale and test this. If you are interested you can also read the full pdf article with all the math involved.

text:
How to Improve Golden Gate Assembly
I've been doing a lot of golden gate assemblies using NEBridge Master Mix and BsaI-HFv2 (also with BbsI; same applies). I'm sure the same tips apply to a non-master mix assembly.
I was originally getting poor complexity and a fair bit of colonies in my negative control, but with the protocol below I'm now getting >5M transformants (based on colonies counted) and nothing on my negative control plates (at least at 1000x dilution).
My negative control is the exact same as the primary sample but I remove one of the middle inserts.
tldr; pre-digesting the backbone, use more enzyme in the rxn, digest again after the assembly, extending the thermocycler protocol, electroporate transform 200+ng of assembly.
Note: I made a lot of protocol changes all at once, so I haven't actually isolated which of the steps are crucial for the improvements.
Golden Gate Assembly:
- I use the NEB Ligation Fidelity Tool for Golden Gate Assembly and make sure I get 100% fidelity for all overhangs. However, I was doing that before switching to the steps outlined below and still getting low positive sample colonies in my negative control plates. u/mrjohns1988 suggested this paper for selecting overhangs sequences.
- Pre-digest you backbone
- 2µg of DNA with BsaI/BbsI (or whatever you use for golden gate).
- Use 2-4µL of restriction enzyme. 37°C overnight (doesn't really matter if you heat inactivate).
- I gel extract + gel cleanup.
- I now use LacZ as the chunk that gets excised to ensure that there aren't any blue colonies on my plates. It's been pretty handy in debugging (I no longer have any blue colonies). I'm not sure why people stopped using LacZ these days; it's barely any extra work to make those plates.
- I used to use a small (
- Reduce the fragment number with pre-assemblies if possible: I was doing 7-9 fragment assemblies into a backbone originally, but only 3 of them were library components, so I did linear pre-assemblies for each library component with 1-2 constant fragments, followed by low-cycle PCR (8 cycles in 200µL reactions using a cheapo homebrew polymerase), and then have only 3 library fragments to assemble into my backbone with a one-pot assembly.
- For the low-cycle PCR: I do a pilot qPCR to get figure out how much template to use for 8 cycles to line up with 50% of the qPCR peak. I find if I go beyond 50% of the qPCR peak then I get multiple bands in a gel, and the reduced cycle number + PCR cleanup kit gives better yield than gel extraction in my hands (given that you loose a bunch of DNA to the other chimeric bands).
- I typically PCR all my fragments from G-Blocks or plasmids. I always run them on a gel to check that they're a clean single band and I gel extract them if they're not (or do a low cycle, high volume PCR reaction as above if I think the PCR Is causing chimeric recombination leading to the extra bands).
- I'm sure you could use G-Blocks directly, but I've always been paranoid I'll run out or that there will be truncated molecules that will reduce fidelity/efficiency, so I end up PCR'ing everything.
- I have found that Prime Star MAX 2 is the most consistent/robust polymerase (though I normally use a higher Ta than the recommended 55°C), with the caveat that the buffer causes its bands to be thicker on a gel so I normally run the gel visualization after PCR cleanup. Q5, SuperFi Platinum II, Kapa HiFi, Phusion are all fine but I find they're more finicky (more double bands on a gel compared to Prime Star), and they take a lot longer to run (I only do 5-10s/kb extension for prime star, whereas the other need 30s). I should mention that I basically always do qPCR (especially for libraries) to avoid weird chimeras or primer-dimers, so adding SYBR might interfere with these polymerases, I haven't actually tested that.
- I use 0.1-0.3pmol (typically 0.25pmol) of each fragement (NEB recommends 0.05pmol each).
- I only use 0.1pmol only when I'm doing like 5 parallel reactions and don't have enough pre-digested backbone for
- I use 1.5-4µL of BsaI-HFv2 (typically 2µL) (NEB recommends 1µL).
- Thermocycler Protocol (I do this even for only 2 or 3 library fragments):
- 37°C for 60min
- 30-60 cycles - cycle number and duration depend on how long I want to wait, I doubt it makes much of a difference. I typically do 45 cycles; 5minute per step and leave it overnight.
- 37°C 2.5-5min [note: this is part of the 30-60 cycles but reddit limits lists to 2 indents]
- 16°C 2.5-5min [note: this is part of the 30-60 cycles but reddit limits lists to 2 indents]
- 37°C 10min
- 60°C 15min
- 4°C ∞
- Post Assembly Digest in the morning:
- Add 1µL BsaI - I suspect this is actually the most important step for reducing negative control colonies.
- 37°C 30-60min
- 60°C 10min - (BsaI heat inactivation is 80°C. T4 ligase is 65°C, but I think NEB suggests that the high PEG concentration doesn't bode well at 65°C, so 60°C is a compromise where BsaI is still highly active but T4 ligase is completely inactive).
- 4°C ∞ - I typically purify immediately after or store @ -20°C until then because T4 ligase is active even at 4°C.
- Purify with SPRI beads or a PCR cleanup kit. Elute in 6.5µL of UP H20 (you'll normally lose 0.5µL to the cleanup gods).
- I tend to average ~50ng/µL (according to nanodrop) after this (though probably only 50% of that DNA is from successful assemblies).
- Electroporate >100ng of plasmid (I typically target >200ng depending on how much DNA I have). You can do 1:10 liquid:cells volume (i.e. 5µL of plasmid for 50µL of cells).
- I typically use 4µL (~200ng @ 50ng/µL) so that if my cells get zapped, then I have ~2µL backup and don't need to repeat the assembly. That only happens like 1 in 20 times though, and I usually repeat the assembly anyways, so probably using all 6µL would be better transformation yield if you're a cowboy.
- I have found transforming with more DNA makes a big difference for increasing positive sample colonies (but increases negative control colonies proportionally, which I believe the extra post-assembly digestion and backbone pre-digestion solve).
- I have used that amount of DNA when electroporating 25µL, 50µL, and 100µL aliquots of cells. 100µL has been working really well for me lately (I haven't actually tested if it gives 4x more colonies than 25µL aliquots).
- Note: I make my own homebrew electrocompetent cells by growing out and washing NEB stable3 cells (they don't sell electro comp stable cells), and the typical transformatione efficiency ~5e9 transformants/µg of pUC19 if I recall correctly.
- Probably doesn't make a difference, but I do the following after taking cells from the -80°C freezer:
- 5 minutes on ice
- Add DNA + flick tube 3-5 times.
- 30s-5min on ice.
- Add cells to cuvette (pre-cool cuvette in -20°C; doubt it makes a difference though)
- Immediately after the pulse I put in 1mL (minus the amount of cells) of SOC recovery media (preheated to 30°C).
- then incubate for 1h at 30°C (I have AAV ITRs so do 30°C instead of 37°C).
- I plate a 1000x and 10,000x dilution and put the rest of the SOC directly into 400mL of liquid culture for midiprep. I wrote more details on that here, including tips for increasing midiprep yield.
Let me know if you have feedback and I can update the list, as I'm sure my goldfish memory will google "how to improve golden gate assembly" in 6 months, and to make ChatGPT's AI lab robot replace us faster.

text:
How to Improve Midiprep Yield
I was getting 10-50µg from zymo midiprep following the standard protocol, and am now getting 150-400µg (1-3µg/µL). [edit: I confirmed the yield with nanodrop and QuBit]
I have a low copy number plasmid and use homebrew NEB Stable3 cells.
I also have AAV ITRs in most of my plasmids, so I can't overgrow them like you could without ITRs.
tldr; use 5-10x the recommended culture volume and shake your tubes more aggressively for longer after adding P2 lysis buffer and P3 neutralizing buffers to ensure cells are completely lysed.
Midiprep Culture Growth: NEB Stable3 @ 30°C + 225RPM
- Inoculate a 5-10mL culture (LB+carb) with transformed E. Coli, then grow for 8h, typically until OD~=2. "transformed E. Coli" can be:
- colony picked from a plate.
- direct from glycerol stock.
- direct from chemical mix'n'go, heat shock, or electroporation transformation.
- I typically use 50-75% of recommended antibiotic, don’t think it makes a difference though. Carb > Amp.
- Make a glycerol stock by mixing 1mL of culture with 1mL of sterilized 50% glycerol.
- Make a starter culture by mixing 1mL of culture with 4mL of LB + 4µL carb; store at 4°C until no longer needed. I do this in case something goes wrong, or I need more yield; I basically repeat the next step and beyond from here.
- Put 1mL of the culture into 200-400mL culture (LB+carb) in a 2L flask (i.e. 5-10x more culture, without compromising 5-20% of flask volume). I think using 400mL cultures is probably the biggest contributor to improved yields.
- You can skip steps 1-4 and it won't make any difference (I've only tested this after electroporation transformation, but that does get incubated for 1h before I put it into a 400mL culture).
- Grow until OD 2-2.5 (sometimes I come in late and it's ~3; i've found this gives higher yield but doesn't seem to recombine the ITRs based on plasmidsaurus ONT). And yes, I check the OD every time; it takes at all then you haven’t spun long enough and are pouring out good bacteria.
- Pour out supernatant. Sometimes the pellet loosens so if you see that happening you have to stop pouring and re-spin so you don’t loose bacteria. I normally pour the supernatant back into the 2L flask it came from, just in case I messed something up, I can just pour it back into the 240mL tube and re-spin. You can leave a small amount (I think this is also another major factor in yield improvement: making sure your cells are fully lysed.
- Use 25-50% more B2 and B3 buffer than suggested. Probably binding buffer too. I admit adding 50% more solution is basically like doing a maxi, and you're also consuming reagents for future preps, so I only do this if we magically have extra buffer leftover from older kits.
- Spin 10min @ 3500g after the P3 yellow buffer following the “low copy number protocol”. Use a p1000 pipette tip to hold the floating lysis crud while you pour the supernatant into the syringe
- Warm elution buffer to 55°C, and let it sit on the matrix for 5-10minutes before spinning.
- I use the recommended 200µL of elution buffer for midi.
- I use ultra pure H20 as the elution buffer so that I can electorporate mammalian cells with it, the elution buffer supplied or TE buffer has salts that may cause arcing.
- Double elute with the same elution buffer (i.d. suck it up from your 1.5mL tube and put it back on the matrix and spin again).
- I find that I end up with 160-180µL afterwards. 20-40µL being lost to the elution gods after the two elution spins.
- If you need higher concentrations, you can leave the tube open overnight (can take a couple days depending on your desired concentration) to let water evaporate or use a SpeedVac vacuum concentrator.
- If you do this, be sure to elute with UP H20, otherwise the salt concentration will increase because the salts won't evaporate with the water.
This probably applies to maxiprep too, but I'd do 1-2L of culture and expect >1mg of DNA. I haven't tried it though.
Some of these tips I got from various other reddit posts (i.e. credit to this one), but these are all compiled together and I've verified it with 10+ midipreps within the last week.
Let me know if you have feedback and I can update the list, as I'm sure my goldfish memory will google "how to improve midiprep yield" in 6 moths.

text:
I am about to lose my sanity
Almost 7 months into my postdoc.
Almost every data point I have delivered thus far has been "too variable". I work with immortalised cell lines, worked with them for the entirety of my PhD. These are not new to me, and their variability is also not new to me.
I joined a lab that lost all of its members except the senior postdoc and PI. I was the first new person to join, and initially I received great 1-1 training with the senior postdoc. Now it's just radio silence. I ask questions, I get re-directed. I cannot seem to connect with them on a professional or a personal level.
I am incredibly defeated and stressed writing this out.
For the past 7 months, I have been told "keep doing more experiments" and "keep doing more repeats", which I have been doing to no avail. I have perfected my techniques, I can do everything with my eyes closed, but I have not been able to account for variability which my PI wants to reduce.
I got frustrated after my meeting with my PI yesterday when I presented data from 2 incredibly demanding weeks and once again get told, "it is inconclusive, repeat it". I asked, look I have been doing these experiments for weeks and months. I went over my experimental setup. And PI goes, well this is not how we set things up.
What? Fucking what?
PI tells me their historical way of setting up experiments to get less variation, which for me is personally an unconventional way of setting up experiments that maximises efficiency over rigor. They explain why it works, why it is not technically "incorrect" to set up experiments in this way. This is why they can knock out an n=3 in 1 week when it was taking me 3 weeks to account for different passages, different plates, different days of seeding!!
My frustration? Before I went to my PI about this, I approached the senior postdoc. I asked how can I improve, please teach me. They went over all these small changes I could do to improve the experiment. I can tell you none of those would have decreased variation THAT MUCH to get a result my PI would have been happy with. They did not mention at all this historical way of setting up experiments.
But now after speaking to PI and learning THIS is their historical way, I feel broken. Because I doubted myself every single step of the way in recent times. We have had weekly meetings and now fortnightly meetings one-on-one where I have shown data and all I get is "it is too inconclusive".
7 months of feeling like a fucking failure, feeling like I am wasting time. It's not like I did not try to make it work. I did!! I put in overtime, I added on workload to keep up. Everything was failing in my hands and the answer was THEIR HISTORICAL METHOD?! How was I supposed to know that unless I ASKED? And I did ask!!! I kept getting a non-answer until YESTERDAY!
I feel so broken. I feel so cheated. I was struggling massively with imposter syndrome in this past few months because nothing felt good enough for my PI who was used to seeing practically 0 variation. I don't even have the energy to do any experiments for the remainder of the week because I feel so defeated and deflated.
I just needed to get this off my chest.

text:
How to be a team player in the lab?
So, here is my problem.
When I started working in a lab, it quickly became clear that I am really independent and "talented" at lab work. So, my supervisors gave me my own projects and only provided guidance; I wasn't working with other students on the same/similar topic or doing experiments with others. This was fine - I loved it.
Now, I am a 3rd-year PhD student (in a different lab). I also started working alone here, which was fine; I feel like I am thriving. My mentor provides guidance, but I am her only PhD student, so I do all the experiments and lab work (basically, we are a 2-person team). But now, I am supposed to mentor other students (BSc and MSc), which means not just teaching them, but allowing them to do some of my experiments, since I run all projects.
And I feel threatened. I fear multiple things.
- I am afraid of them making mistakes. Then there are 2 options:
- They notice it, tell me, and then I have to repeat the experiment/"babysit" them while they repeat it - which I don't have time for. It would be much faster and foolproof to do all the experiments myself.
- They do not notice it, leaving me with false results.
- I am afraid that I will lose results that I could otherwise use for my own papers, dissertation, grants, etc., because they perform the experiments, so basically that is their results from that point.
- Since I am the only PhD student, I have multiple ongoing projects that students can join. However, I do not have the capacity to supervise completely separate projects outside my own scope. Furthermore, I don't have the time to repeat protocols endlessly*, so I worry that mentoring will consume too much of the time I need to generate my own results.
*endlessly = 10-20 times explaining the protocol. E.g.: explaining cell passaging in detail to the same student, because they cannot remember the steps/materials/etc. (This actually happened to me: I had to explain basic passaging over and over because the student refused to take notes, claiming he preferred to learn by observing. Even after 10 sessions, he still didn't know what to use to wash the cells or how to neutralize trypsin.)
How can I overcome these thoughts and feelings? I am really used to working alone and "not sharing" - neither the burdens nor the results.
Also, I feel really stupid for having these feelings and thoughts...

We're testing whether a detection signal is RNA-dependent. We split each sample into three and treat in parallel:
1. DNase (expect signal)
2. RNase cocktail, A (500 U/mL) + T1 (20.000 U/mL) (expect loss of signal)

DNase: 187 ng/µL
RNase: 0.3 ng/µL

Proteinase K treatment (10 min) after digest, in case RNase-inhibitor complexes were clogging the column
Pre-incubating RNase and inhibitor for 30 min at 25 °C before adding to the RNA
Raising inhibitor:RNase ratio to 8:1
Glycerol-only control (same amount as in the inhibitor storage buffer) to check for effects on column binding
TRIzol + precipitation instead of column cleanup
Different new aliquot of Inhibitor
Adding only Inhibitor & no RNase (no loss observed).
Nobody in our lab has worked much with RNA beyond occasional isolations, so we're a bit stuck. Is there something obvious we're missing?

text:
Soil-Transmitted Helminths
I'm a biology student conducting an undergrad thesis on Soil-Transmitted Helminths (STH). I need technical advice in performing the laboratory component of this study from anyone who has expertise in soil research.
So, here's the summary of the procedure:
- collect samples and air-dry for 24 hours.
- sieve through 2.0 mm and 0.125 mm pore size to get 2g.
- place 2g soil in a centrifuge tube and add 10 mL 0.05% polysorbate-80 solution (used to unclump sample).
- centrifuge (1,800 rpm, 10 min)
- discard supernatant
- add 8 mL of prepared 1.20 SG sucrose solution (we used commercially available/market refined white sugar [I was wondering if this was okay]).
- vortex.
- centrifuge (1,800 rpm, 10 min).
- add prepared 1.30 SG sucrose solution to the brim until a meniscus forms.
- place coverslip and wait for eggs to adhere for 5 min.
- add 1 drop lugol's iodine on glass slide.
- place wet underside of coverslip facing down to the glass slide.
- view under microscope.
We performed a trial on this protocol before going to perform it on a larger sample. We observed the following:
- no helminths recovered in collected sample (site = household).
- bubbles found in specimen.

Can you actually cross an ocean inside a whale’s phimosis.
Guys, this is serious. Not a shitpost. I can’t sleep properly because of this philosophical question.
First, the scale. A blue whale’s dick is a fucking massive piece of machinery. The phimosis would turn into a living rubber boat if you somehow climbed inside and sealed it — but only if it’s not erect. Volume-wise an adult man plus a bit of air would fit in there just fine (in theory, idk). But is it waterproof enough? Skin is skin, whales spend their whole lives in salt water, the outer layer is built for that. The inner side though? Mucus, blood vessels, fuck knows what’s going on in there. Would it hold air or would you just slowly fill up with seawater like a sad balloon?
Buoyancy is where the real pain starts. Man plus air pocket versus the density of seawater. You might float, you might sink slowly. Either way you’re not swimming, you’re more like a passive drifting object. Currents exist. Theoretically if you catch the right one you could cover serious distance without any paddling at all. Problem is you can’t paddle. You’re inside a soft biological sleeve. Any movement just jiggles the whole thing. Thrust is basically zero unless you somehow start squeezing jets out of it, which sounds exhausting and also pretty gay.
Oxygen is the hardest part. How much air can you trap in there before the seal fails? A couple of cubic meters max if you’re lucky and the phimosis stretches tight. A human at rest burns through that in hours, not days. Hyperventilate before climbing in? Bring a tube that somehow sticks out? The second you try to surface for air the whole apparatus either collapses or fills up. Plus whales dive. If the owner of the phimosis decides to go deep you’re fucked in every possible way.
Temperature. Whales have a thick blubber layer that holds heat extremely well — the whole body is basically a giant thermos. If the phimosis sits close to the body it could stay pretty warm inside, nothing like the open ocean. The only question is how much of that insulation actually transfers into the pocket itself and whether all the heat just leaks out into the water through the thin membrane.
Another problem is space. Very few people can stay still for long, and even if you manage it your arms and legs will start atrophying. So at some point you might start moving around and accidentally jerk him off from the inside. If you’re really unlucky the dick goes hard, massively reducing your living space. And if you’re not careful you could end up completely alone out in the open ocean.
So theoretically if
the phimosis is big enough and seals properly
you catch a favourable current
you somehow solve the air problem
the whale doesn’t notice or just doesn’t give a fuck
then in theory this shit could actually be pulled off.
Idk guys. The more I think about it the more it feels like one of those things that should be tested under controlled conditions with scientific supervision and a backup boat. For science!!!!

text:
Best compact refrigerated centrifuge for a small clinical research site? Budget ~$5–6k
Hi everyone!
I’m a relatively new Clinical Research Coordinator at a small clinical trial site in the US, and I’ve unexpectedly found myself helping our team select a refrigerated centrifuge. My background is in medicine rather than laboratory equipment, so I’d really appreciate some practical advice from people who have used these machines.
We need a centrifuge for processing blood samples across multiple clinical trials. Our currently identified requirements include:
Refrigerated centrifugation at approximately 4°C
Around 1,500–2,200 ×g (RCF)
Runs of 10–15 minutes
Occasional double-spin processing
Compatibility with approximately 2.5–10 mL blood collection tubes
Preferably a swing-bucket rotor with appropriate adapters
Reliable temperature control, maintenance documentation, and service support
Our vendor has proposed a refurbished Beckman Coulter Allegra X-14R with an SX4750 rotor and adapters for 7–10 mL tubes. The base unit is listed at around $5,250, although we’re still reviewing the final quoted configuration.
My main concern is its size and weight (approximately 128 kg). We have limited bench space, and I’m not sure we need such a large machine for a relatively small clinical research operation.
I also found the Eppendorf 5702 R, which seems much more compact and appears to meet our basic requirements, but a new unit with the appropriate accessories costs roughly $10,000.
For those working in clinical research labs or processing central-lab specimens:
Is the Allegra X-14R overkill for a small research site?
Are there smaller refrigerated swing-bucket centrifuges you’d recommend in the $5–6k range, including reliable refurbished options?
What should we prioritize when buying refurbished — refrigeration performance, rotor condition, calibration, warranty, service availability, or something else?
How important is bench stability and vibration for a machine this heavy?
Are there any specific models you’d recommend avoiding?
We’ll verify the final choice against each study’s laboratory manual, but I’d love to narrow down the options based on real-world experience.
Thanks so much for any suggestions!

text:
IN VITRO SYSTEMATIC REVIEW TOOLKIT
Doing a systematic review on cell-line studies and hit a wall that nobody warned me about.
Every guide I found assumed I was reviewing clinical trials. Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 — the standard tool everyone recommends — asks about things like "allocation concealment" and "blinding of participants." My studies are in vitro experiments. There are no participants. Several of the questions simply don't apply.
So I went looking for the in vitro equivalent and found out there isn't one. No single risk-of-bias tool has been standardised for cell-line studies. The two most commonly recommended — ToxRTool and OHAT — actually assess different aspects of bias, so each one alone only gives you partial coverage. QUIN exists but was built specifically for dentistry. SciRAP was designed for chemical regulation and its own developers say it wasn't meant for systematic reviews.
Researchers are literally still publishing new tools to fill this gap — there was one for antimicrobial studies published this year — because the absence of a standard is considered a methodological flaw in the literature.
I spent a long time piecing together which tool fits which situation, so I made a simple decision tree: you answer a few questions about your study designs and it points you at the right instrument with the reasoning behind it. Also includes the Methods-section wording and answers to the "why didn't you use Cochrane RoB 2" reviewer question, which I got asked.
Free, no signup: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1yVIDcgprC2yKsvI6YiEiE0f9SR-wegUV/view?usp=sharing

Doubts from a student researcher
I’ve recently graduated from undergrad this past summer and I’ve been working in a developmental kidney research lab for almost 3 years now. I can’t help but always wonder if it’s normal to always feel like you know nothing. Honestly it goes beyond that, applying concepts outside of school is so different. I’ve genuinely started feeling like my brain work as a snails pace when I’m in lab.It takes me a forever to even understand what other lab members are telling me or what exactly they are asking me to do. I’m not sure how I can improve because advice online seems to be for an individuals at a higher level. I have a very supportive PI and I’d say I’m passionate and work hard to do my best, but still find it difficult to go beyond just doing what my mentor tells me to do.
Making my own hypothesis about my work feels beyond my reach and I feel like I don’t have really input when we have lab meetings, I can never go beyond just learning data collection and quantification. It’s so embarrassing I literally struggle with basic math sometimes too. I might actually just be an idiot, but can everyone just do mental math?? I’m not sure how many people relate to this, but I just always feel myself lacking.
My doubts start with me not understanding or knowing how to do various parts of protocols or procedures, or maybe my PI and I are trying to address some concerns about my quantification results. Then she’ll ask some questions and explain parts of the biology, and I simply don’t know enough background to give much input. After that I’ll try to think of ways to improve, maybe I can read some review articles and look into the literature more to better understand my work. But in my effort to figure out what I can improve I go down a rabbit whole of thinking about all the things that I can’t do well and eventually I find myself questioning my lack of master of basic skills like language comprehensions and mental math.
Overall my research feels like a lot of technical stuff that I can at least do in the lab, but I guess I really lack a deep understanding and it constantly makes me feel uncomfortable. Does anyone else relate to this, and if so how do you deal with it? I’d really appreciate any input!
